title: Where do consultants go after consulting?
description: The common paths after consulting, from corporate strategy and private equity to start-ups, the public sector and staying to make partner.
hook: Consultants most often move into corporate strategy, general management and operations, private equity and investing, start-ups, and the public or non-profit sector, while some stay and work towards partner. The skills travel well: structured problem solving, comfort with data and clear communication. The best exits are chosen for the skills they build next, not just the title.
body:
The common paths

PathWhat it looks likeWhat it draws on most
Corporate strategy and business developmentWorking on the same kinds of questions from inside one companyMarket analysis, executive communication
General management and operationsMoving from advising to running a team, product or business unitOwnership of recurring metrics, managing people
Private equity and investingEvaluating and improving companies as an investorDue diligence, financial judgement
Start-ups and scale-upsStrategy, operations or chief-of-staff roles, or founding a companySpeed, customer discovery, doing things yourself
Public sector, policy and non-profitsApplying problem solving to social and policy questionsStructuring messy problems, working with many stakeholders

And some people stay, moving up towards principal and partner. Our guide to the consulting career path explains how that ladder and "up or out" work, which is part of why exits are so built into consulting careers.

Why consultants are in demand

Structured problem solving, comfort with data, clear communication and exposure to many industries are useful almost everywhere. Consultants also learn to work with senior people early, to produce under deadline pressure and to turn analysis into a decision. Those are the skills an employer is really hiring when it hires a former consultant.

The gap, which good candidates acknowledge, is usually ownership. Consultants advise; operators live with the consequences. If you move into an operating role, expect to show you can own results over time, not just recommend them.

Choose the next skill, not just the next title

Different exits use different parts of the toolkit. Imagine two consultants who both worked on a retailer's growth strategy. One built the market-entry models and wants to join an internal strategy team. The other led a store pilot and wants to run a regional business. Their experience overlaps, but the evidence they should emphasise differs:

  • The first should show how their analysis changed a strategic decision.
  • The second should show how they handled real constraints and delivered measurable results on the ground.

The same project can support either story. What you choose to highlight should match the job you want next.

A worked example: weighing two offers

Suppose you are choosing between a corporate strategy role and an operations role at a start-up. A simple weighted score makes your priorities explicit. Score each option from 1 to 5 on what matters to you, then weight the criteria. The scores and weights below are illustrative.

CriterionWeightCorporate strategyStart-up operations
Decision ownership30%35
Learning30%44
People management20%24
Stability20%52

Corporate strategy: 0.3 × 3 + 0.3 × 4 + 0.2 × 2 + 0.2 × 5 = 0.9 + 1.2 + 0.4 + 1.0 = 3.5. Start-up: 0.3 × 5 + 0.3 × 4 + 0.2 × 4 + 0.2 × 2 = 1.5 + 1.2 + 0.8 + 0.4 = 3.9. The start-up edges ahead.

The value is not the score itself. It is seeing which weights would flip the answer. If stability mattered most to you, at 50%, with the other weights at 20%, 20% and 10%, corporate strategy scores 4.1 and the start-up 3.2. The decision depends on what you value, so be honest about it. This is the same weighted-criteria logic you use in cases; our weighted averages guide covers the maths.

How to talk about exits in interviews

It is fine to see consulting as one step in a longer journey. But in interviews, focus on why you want the consulting job itself. Interviewers want people who are excited about the work, not just the exit.

Weak: "Consulting is a great springboard, and in two years I'd like to move into private equity."
Strong: "I want to get very good at structuring hard problems and working with senior clients. I don't know yet whether I'll stay long term, but that's exactly what I want to build over the next few years."

The strong answer is honest and keeps the focus on the work. More strong and weak "why consulting" answers show the same idea.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing on title or pay alone. Neither tells you whether the role builds the skills you care about.
  • Leaving with a generic story. "I did strategy projects" is weak. Pick the projects that prove you can do the new job.
  • Ignoring who you will learn from. Ask who your manager will be and what the last person in the role went on to do.
  • Leading with the exit in a consulting interview. Talk about the work first.

Practise now

1. In the weighted score above, what weight on stability (with decision ownership taking the rest of the change) would make the two options tie?

Show the answer

Keep learning at 30% and people management at 20%, and let stability be s and ownership 50% − s. The gap on ownership is 5 − 3 = +2 for the start-up; on people, 4 − 2 = +2, worth 0.2 × 2 = 0.4; on stability, 2 − 5 = −3. The tie needs 2 × (0.5 − s) + 0.4 − 3s = 0, so 1.4 = 5s and s = 28%. Above 28% on stability, corporate strategy wins.

2. A consultant who led a hospital scheduling project wants an operations role at a health-tech start-up. What should their CV and interviews emphasise?

Show the answer

Ownership and delivery: what they changed on the ground, how they worked with nurses and managers, the measurable result (for example, shorter waiting times), and what they did when the plan met reality. Less about the slide deck, more about implementation.

Where to go next

If you are still deciding whether consulting is for you, start with what consultants do day to day and the different types of consulting.
